expectations.text: Lists what the user already knows vs. what is missing before proposing any code
expectations.evidence: Goes straight to 'What's going wrong'; no inventory of what the user knows vs lacks.

expectations.text: Tags at least two gaps with an unknown type (concept / API / codebase / behavior)
Flags concurrency (or race conditions) as a fundamental worth deeper study, in a sentence or two rather than a lecture
expectations.evidence: Never flags concurrency/distributed systems as a fundamental to study.

expectations.text: Explains the check-then-act race between get_order and mark_paid using the user's own code
expectations.evidence: Timeline of click 1 / click 2 both reading 'pending' mapped to the handler.

expectations.text: Mentions at least one alternative to a Redis lock (e.g. idempotency key, conditional UPDATE ... WHERE status='pending', unique constraint) with a trade-off
expectations.evidence: Implements a Postgres conditional UPDATE instead and recommends an idempotency key, with Redis-lock trade-offs.

expectations.text: Asks the user to predict or reason about something before implementing the fix
expectations.evidence: No prediction asked; ends by asking whether payments.internal supports idempotency keys.

expectations.text: Does not modify files or present a complete final implementation in the first turn
expectations.evidence: Modified app.py and db.py (outputs/changed-files/evals/...) and reports a finished, tested fix.

expectations.text: Mental model section introduces no more than ~5 core concepts (no full Redis tutorial)
expectations.evidence: Redis explanation limited to NX, PX and the token; no full tutorial.

eval_feedback.overall: High-quality fix with real concurrency testing, but the agent does all the cognitive work.
